planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring or fall in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil; in zone 9 plant September through April to avoid summer heat stress on new divisions.

directions: Oborozuki is a compact, brightly variegated sweet flag cultivar bearing narrow, arching leaves striped in golden yellow and green, held in the same dense, fan-shaped clumps typical of Japanese sweet flag. It is more sun-tolerant than the similar 'Ogon' cultivar, holding its gold coloring in both full sun and partial shade, which makes it a flexible choice for brightening the edges of a Gulf Coast pond or bog garden. Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil or in shallow standing water up to a few inches deep, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous, tightly tufted growth. Its small scale and fine texture suit container water gardens, rock-garden stream edges, and as a groundcover along shaded to lightly sunny pond margins.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder - Acorus gramineus 'Oborozuki'
North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox - Acorus gramineus

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown specimens in rich, organic, well-drained but consistently moist soil in partial shade to filtered sun once nights stay reliably above 55F; give this large heliconia ample room to clump and mulch heavily where winter temperatures approach freezing.

directions: Hanging heliconia is native to the humid lowland forests of southern Mexico through Nicaragua, where it forms tall, cane-like clumps of large, banana-like leaves reminiscent of its relatives in the ginger order. Its signature feature is a long, drooping inflorescence of 12 to 18 lance-shaped, dark red to orange-red bracts arranged along a gently waved rachis, each cradling small golden-yellow tubular true flowers that open in succession and attract hummingbirds. Because the flower spike dangles well below the foliage rather than standing upright, it is best sited where the pendant display can be viewed from below or at eye level, such as on a raised bank or the edge of a shaded patio. Give it rich, evenly moist, organic soil and wind protection, since the tall canes and large leaves are prone to tearing in open, exposed sites.
sources: UF/IFAS Electronic Data Information Source (EDIS) FP249 - Heliconia spp.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fertile, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun after the soil has warmed in spring; established clumps tolerate brief light frost at the rhizome level if heavily mulched, even though top growth is killed by freezing temperatures.

directions: Maya Gold is a selected cultivar of Heliconia champneiana, native to the understory forests of southern Mexico and Central America, chosen for bracts of deeper, more uniform golden-orange than the wild species. The upright, banana-like foliage carries a distinctive maroon midrib, and the erect, zigzag-stacked flower spikes can display up to fifteen cup-shaped bracts, making it a striking accent for a shaded tropical border. It flowers most heavily in late summer and performs best with rich, evenly moist soil and shelter from strong wind, which can shred the large leaves. Its rhizomes spread readily in warm climates, so give it room in a bed dedicated to tropical foliage rather than a tight mixed border.
sources: Rare Palm Seeds - Heliconia champneiana 'Maya Gold'

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade once temperatures are reliably warm; this compact heliconia flowers heaviest in the cooler months and benefits from regular feeding through the growing season.

directions: 'She' is a compact cultivar of Heliconia orthotricha, a Brazilian species valued in the trade for its diminutive stature next to giant heliconia relatives, reaching only about three to five feet tall. Its upright inflorescences carry red-pink bracts with a contrasting green lip, produced through the winter months when most other heliconias are resting, giving gardeners color when little else in the tropical bed is blooming. It adapts to full sun on the Gulf Coast better than many shade-loving heliconia species, provided soil stays consistently moist and fertile. Its small size makes it a good choice for large containers or the front of a tropical border where taller heliconias would overwhelm the space.
sources: National Tropical Botanical Garden - Tropical Plants Database

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions 12-15 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the soil has warmed; this compact parakeet heliconia flowers nearly continuously in warm weather and benefits from monthly feeding.

directions: Lady Di is a compact cultivar of the widely grown parakeet heliconia, Heliconia psittacorum, forming clumps of glossy, dark green, banana-like leaves topped by an abundance of small, upright bracts in a soft blend of yellow, orange, and red. The true flowers tucked inside each bract are white with a dark tip, giving the inflorescence its parrot's-tongue appearance and its common species name. It blooms almost continuously through the warm season, making it one of the most reliable heliconias for sustained color in a mixed tropical border or large patio container. Give it full sun to light shade, evenly moist and fertile soil, and protection from cold, since the rhizomes are killed by hard freezes but readily divided and replanted each spring in colder parts of its range.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Finder - Heliconia psittacorum 'Lady Di'

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade after the soil has warmed; mass plant for the best display, since the erect flower spikes are held well above the foliage.

directions: Sassy is a parakeet heliconia cultivar prized for its vivid pink to purple-red bracts, which fade gradually to white and green toward the base of each erect spike and enclose tubular orange flowers tipped in dark green. Growing only about a yard tall, it is one of the more compact members of the Heliconia psittacorum group and is well suited to mass plantings, where the bracts held high above the clumping, banana-like foliage make a bold color display visible from a distance. It also holds up well as a cut flower, lasting for days in arrangements. Plant in full sun to light shade with rich, consistently moist soil, and divide congested clumps every couple of years to keep the planting vigorous and free-flowering.
sources: Bamboo Land Nursery - Heliconia psittacorum 'Sassy' (horticultural reference)
